paragraphs.text: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy-2 (FAME2) is an autosomal dominant disorder of familial cortical reflex myoclonus. Patients have a shivering movement of the hands brought on by action, along with jerking of the upper limbs, and these are variably associated with focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures. In many patients the main feature is a mild postural hand tremor that resembles essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus. A minority of patients have borderline or moderately impaired cognition, and the myoclonus often worsens in advanced age.

paragraphs.text: Guerrini et al. (2001) described a pedigree with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME) in which 8 individuals had a nonprogressive disorder with onset between the ages of 12 and 50 years. All patients had mainly distal, semicontinuous rhythmic myoclonus and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and 3 also had complex partial seizures. Most individuals had seizures only rarely and had a normal cognitive level. However, the 3 individuals with intractable seizures had mild mental retardation. All patients had frontotemporal as well as generalized interictal EEG abnormalities. Electrophysiologic findings included an enhanced C-reflex at rest and high-amplitude somatosensory and visual evoked potentials. In patients, the resting motor threshold to transcranial magnetic stimulation was significantly reduced, and the post-MEP silent period was significantly shortened (101 ms vs 137 ms in controls). In 5 patients, EEG-EMG coherence at 8 to 25 Hz over the contralateral rolandic area, with EEG preceding EMG by 8 to 15 ms, suggested that the myoclonus was of cortical origin. Ipsilateral coherence in 2 patients suggested transcallosal spread. The authors suggested that the disorder involves diffuse cortical hyperexcitability, particularly of frontotemporal circuits.

paragraphs.text: Labauge et al. (2002) reported a 4-generation European family with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME) in which 10 living and 3 deceased relatives were affected. The 10 living patients had a mean age at onset of 41 years (range, 30-60 years). Affected individuals had adult-onset myoclonus of the extremities, and 8 of the 13 had generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Electrophysiologic studies confirmed the diagnosis of FAME in the 5 patients studied.

paragraphs.text: Striano et al. (2005) reported a 5-generation family from Naples, Italy, with cortical tremor, myoclonus, and epilepsy. Eleven members, aged 24 to 56 years (mean, 39.2 years), had hand tremor and myoclonus, and 6 also had generalized seizures. Electrophysiologic study showed cortical reflex myoclonus in all affected family members. Three presymptomatic members had giant somatosensory evoked potential components and an enhanced long loop reflex I. After 1.5 years of follow-up, all 3 had developed hand tremor and upper-limb myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: Suppa et al. (2009) reported an Italian family with familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy. Affected members had limb and voice tremor, seizures, and myoclonus of the eyelids during blinking. Neurophysiologic findings suggested increased excitability of the primary motor cortex, with normal sensorimotor integration. Neuropsychological testing showed visuospatial impairment, which the authors suggested might be due to temporal lobe dysfunction.

paragraphs.text: Crompton et al. (2012) reported a 6-generation FAME kindred of European descent, ascertained in New Zealand and Australia, with 55 affected members. All had fine hand tremor, which typically began in adolescence (median age, 15 years; range, 4-60 years). Proximal myoclonus was present in 44 of 55 (80%) and began later than the hand tremor (median age, 17 years; range, 5-60 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred in 8 of 55 (15%), with a median age at onset of 43.5 years (range, 18-76 years). Neurophysiologic testing confirmed features of cortical reflex myoclonus. The most common phenotype was a mild postural hand tremor resembling essential tremor, combined with subtle proximal myoclonus. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were uncommon and occurred around sleep onset after severe generalized myoclonus.

paragraphs.text: De Fusco et al. (2014) studied 2 ADCME families from Tuscany. Family A was the 5-generation family in which the ADCME locus had previously been mapped, and its clinical features closely resembled those of family B. In family B, all affected individuals had postural myoclonus of the hands and upper limbs. Cortical tremor was the presenting symptom in every case and appeared between 18 and 50 years of age. Epilepsy occurred in all affected individuals except 1 (IV:1, a 29-year-old woman with onset at 18 years). Generalized tonic-clonic seizures were seen in individuals I:2, II:4, III:2, and III:5. Two patients (III:2 and III:5) also had drug-resistant focal motor or complex partial seizures. Patient III:2 had a borderline cognitive level, whereas the other affected individuals had normal intelligence. Brain MRI was normal in the 3 patients examined. None of the ADCME patients had evidence of cardiovascular disease. Two of the oldest mutation carriers developed age-related dementia.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) tabulated clinical data from 21 FAME2 families and 1 singleton case. Fifteen families were Italian. The others were Australian/New Zealand of European ancestry (family 1), Iraqi of Sephardic Jewish ancestry, Israeli of Sephardic Jewish ancestry, South African of European ancestry, French/Spanish, and French, and the singleton case was Syrian. Myoclonus or cortical tremor was present in nearly all affected individuals studied. The proportion with tonic-clonic seizures varied between families, from 8 of 55 in family 1 to all affected members in families 2, 3, 4, 14, and 17. Focal seizures were infrequent and were absent in most families. Age at onset also varied between families: it was 12 years in family 6, 2 to 18 years in family 3, and 41 years in the French/Spanish family 19. In the large Australian/New Zealand family 1, the authors found evidence of anticipation, with a median age at onset of 30 years in generation III, 17 years in generation IV, and 12 years in generation V.

paragraphs.text: Corbett et al. (2019) analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from affected members of 3 FAME families using ExpansionHunter and exSTRa. They identified an expansion of the endogenous ATTTT repeat, with an inserted ATTTC repeat, in the first intron of the STARD7 gene within the FAME2 interval on chromosome 2. The ATTTC repeat was absent from whole-genome sequencing data of 69 controls. The authors developed a repeat-primed PCR assay and used it to detect the expansion in 137 of 137 affected individuals from 16 independently reported FAME2 families worldwide. Overall, the ATTTC expansion segregated in 158 of 158 affected individuals from 22 FAME pedigrees. Two of 24 tested individuals without a FAME diagnosis carried the expansion and were likely presymptomatic. The expansion was not amplified in 28 control DNA samples. Among family members with an uncertain FAME diagnosis, usually tremor alone, 8 of 13 carried the expansion. In family 1, 2 individuals with an uncertain diagnosis who tested negative did not share the affected haplotype. Corbett et al. (2019) also screened 52 unrelated patients with generalized epilepsy and tremor or with adult-onset myoclonic epilepsy and found the expansion in only 1, a Syrian singleton case. Long-read sequencing showed that the pathogenic allele had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n. In one patient, a SMRT read contained 274 AAATG and 387 AAAAT repeats, whereas a nanopore read contained 345 AAATG and 390 AAAAT repeats, suggesting somatic variation in repeat size. In a second patient (family 5, III-37), a single nanopore read spanned 588 AAATG and 340 AAAAT repeats, 4,645 bp in total length.

paragraphs.text: In transfected HeLa cells, De Fusco et al. (2014) found that mutant alpha-2B-adrenergic receptor (alpha-2B-AR) localized normally to the plasma membrane and was internalized in an arrestin-3-dependent manner, like the wildtype receptor. In coimmunoprecipitation studies, however, the mutant receptor failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin. After 10 minutes of epinephrine stimulation, spinophilin binding to the mutant receptor fell back to baseline, whereas binding to the wildtype receptor remained elevated. In Xenopus oocytes, spinophilin increased the EC50 for epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling through wildtype alpha-2B-AR but not through the mutant receptor. The authors concluded that the mutation increases the intensity of Ca(2+) signaling, a gain-of-function effect caused by loss of the spinophilin interaction. They proposed that the resulting cortical hyperexcitability might arise from impaired GABAergic inhibition. However, Corbett et al. (2019) later concluded that the ADRA2B allele is not causative (see MOLECULAR GENETICS).

paragraphs.text: In affected members of 2 Tuscan families with autosomal dominant cortical myoclonus and epilepsy (ADCME), De Fusco et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous in-frame insertion/deletion in the ADRA2B gene: c.675_686delTGGTGGGGCTTTinsGTTTGGCAG, resulting in p.His225_Leu229delinsGlnPheGlyArg. The change replaced 5 amino acids (HGGAL) with 4 new ones (QFGR). In family A, the indel segregated completely with the disease. It was not found in 575 Tuscan controls or in public databases. The 2 families shared the same disease haplotype, suggesting a common ancestor. In functional studies, the mutant receptor failed to form a stable complex with spinophilin, and spinophilin did not modulate epinephrine-stimulated calcium signaling through the mutant receptor. The authors interpreted this as a gain-of-function effect.

paragraphs.text: Using a repeat-primed PCR assay, Corbett et al. (2019) found the STARD7 intronic ATTTC repeat expansion in affected members of FAME2 families of Italian, Iraqi Sephardic Jewish, Israeli Sephardic Jewish, South African European, French/Spanish, and French ancestry. They also found it in 1 Syrian singleton case among 52 unrelated patients with generalized epilepsy and tremor or adult-onset myoclonic epilepsy. Overall, the expansion segregated in 158 of 158 affected individuals from 22 FAME pedigrees and was not amplified in 28 control DNA samples. Two of the Italian families (families 4 and 15) also carried the ADRA2B indel previously reported by De Fusco et al. (2014). Long-read sequencing showed that the pathogenic allele had the structure (AAATG)n(AAAAT)n, and differing repeat counts between sequencing reads from one patient suggested somatic variation in repeat size. STARD7 transcript and protein levels were not altered in patient fibroblasts.
